tldr: By mapping nonlinear dynamics to a linear latent space using Koopman operators and eliminating state variables into an action-only quadratic program, this work realizes ultra-fast, microsecond-scale MPC via precompilation. Combining differentiable optimization with DAgger enables control-aware dynamics learning, showing overwhelming speed and performance across applications ranging from microcontrollers to 200-drone swarm GPU control and 2048D visual world models.
hero_caption: Overview of $\mu$MPC application scenarios. It achieves fast control across diverse platforms, from safety filtering for a 4096D quadruped robot (A) and real-time horizon-75 MPC on a 168 MHz microcontroller (Crazyflie) (B), to rope and cube manipulation on physical arms (C, D) and multi-agent collision-avoidance planning for over 150 drones and 7 mobile robots (E, F).
overview:
Nonlinear model predictive control (MPC) is a powerful tool in robotics because it computes optimal actions while explicitly handling constraints. However, when the problem dimension or prediction horizon grows, computational cost explodes. This makes real-time deployment extremely difficult on small robots with limited compute or for visual world models with thousands of latent dimensions.

To tackle this, the authors focus on Koopman operator theory, which maps nonlinear dynamics to an infinite-dimensional linear space. By learning the nonlinear model as a globally linear latent representation, they express outputs over the entire horizon purely in terms of the input sequence, completely condensing out the latent state trajectory. This yields the Koopman-Compiled QP (KC-QP), where the optimization variables are restricted exclusively to the input sequence.

Furthermore, they discovered that the primal update operator—based on the objective Hessian—remains constant regardless of changing goals and constraints, allowing it to be precomputed (precompiled) offline. Online optimization is thus compressed into simple matrix-vector products and element-wise clippings (projections), completely removing the need for online matrix refactorizations. In addition, by integrating this ultra-fast QP into the training loop as a differentiable layer (DiffQP) and combining it with DAgger to collect states visited by the policy, they established a learning method that enhances closed-loop control performance rather than merely minimizing state prediction errors.

Empirical evaluations demonstrate long-horizon control on a 168 MHz microcontroller in 24 ms, quadruped control with a 4096D model in under 5 ms, sub-millisecond (0.4 ms) visuomotor planning using a 2048D visual world model, and collision-aware planning for 200 quadrotors on a GPU at over 30 Hz. Compared to existing methods, $\mu$MPC achieves up to $108\times$ faster constrained MPC and $1907\times$ faster visuomotor planning, establishing a new real-time control foundation from edge devices to cloud GPUs.
contributions: Proposed the KC-QP formulation, which leverages learned Koopman linear dynamics to analytically eliminate state trajectories and compress decision variables strictly into inputs ($Hn_u$ dimensions).

Developed a fixed-operator primal-dual solver that requires no matrix refactorization even under changing goals or constraint relinearization, running fast iterations using only matrix-vector products and projections.

Integrated parallelizable KC-QPs as differentiable optimization into the training loop alongside DAgger, establishing a method to learn high-dimensional latent dynamics directly tied to control performance.

Demonstrated microsecond- to millisecond-scale control performance across diverse hardware and tasks, ranging from a 168 MHz microcontroller and desktop CPUs to embedded edge devices and GPU swarm control.

sections.heading: Why Ultra-Fast Microsecond-Scale MPC Matters Now
sections.summary: Real-time robot control often hits barriers due to compute limits and computational explosions from high-dimensional models. This paper presents $\mu$MPC, an MPC framework that pushes expensive algebraic operations offline via Koopman linearization, leaving only simple operations online.
sections.details:
Modern robot control demands strict real-time performance. Small embedded platforms like drones face severe processor and power limits, while whole-body control for quadrupeds requires solving high-dimensional optimizations in an instant. Furthermore, visual planning—which plans actions directly from camera images—requires repeatedly unrolling (rolling out) world models with thousands of latent dimensions for every action candidate, making computational cost a decisive bottleneck for real-world deployment.

As prediction horizons lengthen or constraints become more complex, conventional nonlinear MPC consumes massive amounts of time on online linearization and large-scale matrix factorizations. Recent linearization approaches using Koopman operators also face challenges; handling nonlinear constraints often demands repeated online matrix recalculations, failing to deliver the promised theoretical speedups.

Another major challenge is model learning for control. Traditional dynamics learning focuses primarily on state prediction accuracy (minimizing prediction error). This makes it fragile to distribution shifts (covariate shifts) induced by the controller, frequently causing control failure even when predictions look accurate.

$\mu$MPC was proposed to break through these barriers. By fully exploiting the linear structure of the learned Koopman model, it analytically eliminates state variables, precompiling the problem into a quadratic program (KC-QP) optimized over inputs alone. Because the online primal-dual method reuses a fixed operator whose matrix inverse is computed offline, it can solve problems using only matrix-vector products and projections even as constraints shift. Furthermore, leveraging this ultra-fast execution, the QP itself is made differentiable and embedded into the training loop to directly optimize control performance.

sections.heading: Lineage and Pitfalls of Koopman Methods, Differentiable Control, and World Models
sections.summary: This section reviews computational bottlenecks in existing Koopman MPC, differentiable control, and visual world model planning. The proposed approach fundamentally resolves these bottlenecks through precompilation, state elimination, and fixed-operator reuse.
sections.details:
### Limitations of Koopman MPC and Fast Optimal Control
While Koopman operator methods that lift nonlinear systems into an infinite-dimensional linear space match well with linear MPC, prior works suffered non-negligible online computational overheads. For instance, approaches relying on fixed dictionary functions struggle to map nonlinear costs and constraints into QPs. Methods that condense decision variables often cater strictly to box input constraints or leave observation-space decision variables behind. While exploiting sparsity and GPU parallelization has advanced fast MPC, repeated matrix refactorizations were still required at every sequential linearization step.

### Dynamics Learning via Differentiable Control
Works that make constrained control problems differentiable for end-to-end learning (such as DiffMPC) have emerged, but repeatedly solving expensive nonlinear MPCs and backpropagating through them in a training loop is computationally prohibitive. Prior works like KCPO were limited to box constraints. $\mu$MPC makes an efficient KC-QP tailored for finite-horizon tracking differentiable, combining it with the imitation learning technique DAgger (aggregating data by having an expert relabel trajectories generated by the policy). This scales control-oriented learning without running heavy nonlinear optimizations.

### World Models and Latent Space Planning
Recent visual world models (e.g., DINO-WM and LeWorldModel) repeatedly roll out candidate action sequences in high-dimensional nonlinear latent spaces, optimizing via sampling-based methods such as CEM. These are computationally heavy, making millisecond-level planning out of reach. In contrast, $\mu$MPC deliberately learns latent dynamics as a linear structure and precompiles the entire horizon's response into a single compact KC-QP. This completely bypasses iterative rollouts and achieves sub-millisecond visual planning.

sections.heading: Problem Formulation: Constrained Nonlinear Optimal Control
sections.summary: This section defines the finite-horizon optimal control problem for discrete-time nonlinear systems targeted in this work. Nonlinear state and task constraints are locally linearized around a nominal trajectory, introducing margins to account for model errors.
sections.details:
This paper considers a discrete-time nonlinear system $x_{k+1} = f(x_k, u_k)$ with state $x_k$ and control input $u_k$. At each control step, the goal is to track a target $y^{\rm goal}$ with a task-relevant output $y_k = S_y x_k$ ($S_y = I$ when using the full state) while satisfying state, task, and input constraints over a horizon $H$, seeking the input sequence $U = [u_0^\top, \dots, u_{H-1}^\top]^\top$.

Nonlinear constraints are locally linearized via first-order Taylor expansions around the current nominal trajectory. To absorb neglected higher-order terms and prediction errors from the learned dynamics model, non-negative margins $\Delta_k, \Delta_f$ are introduced to tighten the constraint boundaries beforehand.

However, because the dynamics $f$ are nonlinear, solving this directly would require complex nonlinear optimization online. This work aims to replace the nonlinear dynamics with a high-dimensional, globally linear latent space model, pushing all expensive algebraic operations offline (precomputation) and reshaping online execution into fixed linear algebra and simple projection operations.

sections.heading: Core of μMPC: Ultra-Fast Execution via Precompilation and Fixed Operators
sections.summary: By expressing the Koopman linear model outputs purely in terms of the input sequence, state variables are eliminated to derive the action-only KC-QP. Furthermore, precomputing a fixed primal operator derived from the objective compresses online computation into matrix-vector products and projections.
sections.details:
### IV-A & IV-B Learned Dynamics and Precomputed Maps
The physical state $x_k$ is mapped to a latent state $z_k$ using an encoder $z_k = \operatorname{enc}_\theta(x_k)$. In the latent space, transitions follow linear matrices $A, B$ ($z_{k+1} = A z_k + B u_k$), and an affine decoder maps back to the physical space via $x_k = C z_k + c$. At each MPC step, the encoder runs only for the current initial state $z_0$; all subsequent horizon predictions rely purely on linear operations.

Thanks to this linear structure, the latent and physical state trajectories over the entire horizon $H$ can be written analytically as affine combinations of $z_0$ and the input sequence $U$. The method constructs operators $F_y, G_y$ offline to express the task output trajectory $Y = [y_1^\top, \dots, y_H^\top]^\top$ as $Y = F_y z_0 + G_y U + c_y$. This completely eliminates the need to keep high-dimensional latent state trajectories as decision variables in the optimization.

### IV-C & IV-D Koopman-Compiled QP (KC-QP) and Fixed-Operator Solver
Substituting the expression for output trajectory $Y$ into the objective function and linearized constraints condenses the optimization into a quadratic program (KC-QP) where the input sequence $U$ is the sole decision variable. The number of decision variables is completely independent of the latent dimension $n_z$, scaling only as $q = H n_u$, the product of input dimension and horizon length.

To solve this KC-QP, a specialized Primal-Dual Proximal Method was constructed. Dual variables (Lagrange multipliers) update via projected gradient ascent on constraint violations. The primal update for $U$ incorporates a proximal term (step size $\rho$), turning it into an unconstrained, strongly convex quadratic minimization with a closed-form solution. Crucially, the primal Hessian matrix $K = \mathcal{H} + \rho I$ depends solely on the learned model, horizon, weights, and $\rho$—it does not depend on the constraint matrix $M$ or boundary vector $r(z_0)$ at all!

Consequently, $K^{-1}$ can be computed once offline and stored in memory. The exact same matrix can be reused online even if target values change or constraints are relinearized. Online computation reduces to simple matrix-vector products and element-wise non-negative projections (clipping), dropping per-iteration complexity to $\mathcal{O}(q^2 + mq)$.

### IV-E Differentiable QP (DiffQP) and Learning with DAgger
To make the Koopman model yield effective control inputs rather than just predicting states, KC-QP is placed directly inside the training loop. Given expert demonstrations, the finite-horizon tracking QP is solved, and by differentiating through the QP, the encoder and system matrices $(A, B, C, c)$ are updated so that the optimal input sequence $\widehat{U}$ matches expert inputs $U$. In addition, DAgger iterations—where trajectories generated by the intermediate controller are executed in simulation and added back for retraining—are adopted to effectively mitigate distribution shift caused by the controller.

sections.heading: From Microcontrollers to GPUs: Validating Blazing Speed and Scalability
sections.summary: Experiments span small microcontrollers (Crazyflie), bipedal/quadruped locomotion, drone swarms, and visual world model manipulation. The method achieves up to 108× speedups over baselines, sub-millisecond visual planning, and real-time collision avoidance for 200 agents.
sections.details:
### V-A–V-C Drone Control and Edge Deployment
In 2D and 3D quadrotor control, $\mu$MPC achieved median solve times of 23 to 128 $\mu$s on a desktop CPU. In 3D obstacle avoidance ($H=100$), it was $2.3\times$ faster than acados/HPIPM, $19\times$ faster than OSQP on the same condensed QP, and over $100\times$ faster than GPU-ADMM SQP. On edge devices like the Raspberry Pi 5 and Jetson Orin Nano, control-constrained MPC took under 3.2 ms, and obstacle-constrained MPC finished in a few milliseconds.

Ablation studies (Table IV) revealed that training with pure prediction loss yielded only a 3.7% goal-reaching rate ($H=75$), whereas adding DiffQP surged this to 97.7%. Incorporating DAgger further maintained over 95% success even over a long horizon ($H=125$).

Furthermore, deploying $\mu$MPC with $H=75$ (300 decision variables) onboard a compute-constrained Crazyflie MCU (Cortex-M4F, 168 MHz) yielded an execution time of 24.57 ms, consistently maintaining stable physical flight within deadline constraints.

### V-C 5 Multi-Agent Swarm Control on GPU
In a task where 200 quadrotors navigate to goals while avoiding collisions, each vehicle's KC-QP was batched onto a GPU. Using Jacobi-style Iterative Best Response (IBR), trajectories of other agents are treated as time-varying obstacle constraints. As the fleet quadrupled from 50 to 200 drones, latency increased by only $2.66\times$ (from 12.1 ms to 32.1 ms), maintaining real-time control frequencies above 30 Hz and goal-reaching rates above 98%.

### V-D Whole-Body Quadruped Locomotion
Using a Unitree Go2 (61D state, 12 torque inputs), a massive 4096D Koopman model was built to evaluate whole-body control. At $H=100$, $\mu$MPC computed solutions in 4.82 ms, running $1.5\times$ faster than MPX (iLQR-based) and $4.7\times$ faster than GPU-ADMM SQP. It also ran in 24–38 ms on a Jetson Orin Nano. Operating as a safety filter for obstacle avoidance, it generated safe evasive maneuvers in real time where nominal policies collided.

### V-E Visual Planning with World Models
For dual-arm rope manipulation and Reacher tasks using raw camera frames, ViT-encoded features were mapped into a 2048D Koopman linear model. Rope manipulation was planned in 0.725 ms and Reacher in 0.427 ms (both sub-millisecond), reaching success rates of 94% and 62%, respectively. This vastly outperformed CEM sampling world models (LeWM at 24%, Fast-LeWM at 46%). On physical Kuka iiwa cube manipulation, DiffQP training enabled the policy to correctly acquire the control inputs needed for lifting.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Outlook: New Frontiers in Ultra-Fast Control
sections.summary: By pairing precompiled fixed operators with differentiable learning, $\mu$MPC opens the door to solving high-dimensional, nonlinear MPC in microseconds to milliseconds. Future work includes automating practical constraint margins.
sections.details:
This paper presented $\mu$MPC, a framework unifying scalable Koopman dynamics learning with ultra-fast constrained MPC. By formulating an action-only KC-QP that eliminates state trajectories and introducing a fixed primal operator precomputable offline, it compresses online optimization strictly into matrix-vector products and projections.

This removes the need to refactor matrices online even when goals shift or constraints are relinearized, demonstrating remarkable performance across 4096D quadruped control, 2048D visual world model planning, long-horizon MCU control, and 200-drone GPU swarm control. The training pipeline combining DiffQP and DAgger was also proven essential for closing the gap in closed-loop control performance.

Nonetheless, the authors point out several limitations and directions for future research. Hyperparameters such as latent dimensionality, encoder architectures, and training horizons currently rely on empirical tuning, highlighting the need for scaling laws that theoretically capture the relationship between model capacity and closed-loop performance. Addressing minor constraint violations when iterations are truncated under strict time budgets and establishing rigorous probabilistic calibrations for constraint tightening margins ($\Delta$) to guarantee theoretical safety remain vital topics for future work.

takeaways: Lifting dynamics into a linear latent space (Koopman) and condensing out state variables caps QP decision variables to input dimension × horizon length, regardless of how large the latent dimension is.

Because the primal update Hessian in the primal-dual proximal method is constraint-independent, precomputing its inverse offline (precompilation) reduces online computation to matrix-vector products and clipping.

Directly optimizing control input tracking by differentiating through the QP (DiffQP) and gathering self-generated state distributions with DAgger are vital for closed-loop success beyond mere prediction error minimization.
Deliberately learning linear latent dynamics for visual world models removes the need for heavy sampling searches like CEM, enabling sub-millisecond visual planning.
limitations: Selecting latent dimensions (e.g., 2048D or 4096D) and encoder architectures still relies on empirical trial and error, as unified design principles or scaling laws have not yet been established.
Enforcing a fixed upper limit on iterations to ensure real-time guarantees introduces the risk of minor constraint violations under tight constraint regimes when compute is truncated.
Constraint tightening margins ($\Delta$) used to compensate for linearization and modeling errors remain manually tuned heuristics, lacking theoretical safety guarantees or probabilistic calibration.
